# LU decomposition {#sec-lu-decomposition}

[Core]{.level-badge .core}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## In this chapter you will

- factorise a square matrix as $\M{A} = \M{L}\M{U}$ by recording the multipliers of Gaussian elimination
- solve $\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}$ from the factors, by forward and back substitution
- explain why factorising once saves time when there are many right-hand sides
- use the factorisation $\M{P}\M{A} = \M{L}\M{U}$ that software computes, with its row swaps
:::

**Builds on** @sec-multiplication, @sec-gaussian-elimination.

Gaussian elimination (@sec-gaussian-elimination) computes a multiplier for every entry it clears, uses it once, and throws it away. This chapter keeps them. Stored in a matrix $\M{L}$, the multipliers turn elimination into a **factorisation** $\M{A} = \M{L}\M{U}$: the matrix written as a product of a lower triangular matrix and an upper triangular one. It is the form in which every serious solver actually does elimination, because once $\M{A}$ has been factorised, each new right-hand side can be solved in a tiny fraction of the time.

## Build intuition

The row reduction stepper is now in LU mode. It carries out ordinary elimination on the right, where $\M{A}$ gradually turns into $\M{U}$. Each multiplier it uses is written into $\M{L}$ on the left, in the position of the entry it cleared.

## The ideas

### Elimination is a factorisation

Take
$$
\M{A} = \mat{2 & 1 & 1 \\ 4 & 3 & 3 \\ 8 & 7 & 9}.
$$
Elimination uses three multipliers: $R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - 2R_1$ and $R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - 4R_1$ clear column 1, then $R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - 3R_2$ clears column 2, leaving the upper triangular
$$
\M{U} = \mat{2 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2}.
$$
Put each multiplier $m_{ij}$ in row $i$, column $j$ of a matrix with 1s on the diagonal and zeros above it:
$$
\M{L} = \mat{1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 3 & 1}.
$$
Then $\M{L}\M{U} = \M{A}$, as you can check by multiplying.

Here is why it works. Elimination finishes each row of $\M{U}$ by subtracting multiples of the rows of $\M{U}$ above it. Row 3, for example, became row 3 of $\M{A}$ minus $4 \times$ (row 1 of $\M{U}$) minus $3 \times$ (row 2 of $\M{U}$). Turned round,
$$
\text{row 3 of } \M{A} = 4 \times (\text{row 1 of } \M{U}) + 3 \times (\text{row 2 of } \M{U}) + 1 \times (\text{row 3 of } \M{U}),
$$
which is row 3 of $\M{L}$ times $\M{U}$, by the row view of multiplication (@sec-multiplication). The same holds for every row. So:

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## LU decomposition
If Gaussian elimination on a square matrix $\M{A}$ needs no row swaps, then $\M{A} = \M{L}\M{U}$, where $\M{U}$ is the upper triangular result of elimination and $\M{L}$ is the lower triangular matrix with 1s on its diagonal and the multipliers $m_{ij}$ below it.
:::

A proof is in @sec-proofs-lu-decomposition. If $\M{A}$ is invertible, these factors are the only ones of this shape.

### Solving with the factors

To solve $\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}$, write it as $\M{L}(\M{U}\vect{x}) = \vect{b}$ and split it into two triangular systems, with $\vect{y} = \M{U}\vect{x}$:

1. solve $\M{L}\vect{y} = \vect{b}$ by **forward substitution**, from the top down;
2. solve $\M{U}\vect{x} = \vect{y}$ by **back substitution**, from the bottom up, as in @sec-gaussian-elimination.

Forward substitution is back substitution turned upside down. Since $\M{L}$ has 1s on its diagonal, the first equation gives $y_1 = b_1$ directly, and each later one gives
$$
y_i = b_i - \sum_{j=1}^{i-1} \ell_{ij}\,y_j.
$$
In fact, $\vect{y}$ is exactly what the right-hand side would have turned into if it had been carried along during elimination. Forward substitution just replays the stored multipliers on it.

::: {#ex-lu-decomposition-1 .callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
### Example 1: two right-hand sides

Use the factors of $\M{A} = \mat{2 & 1 & 1 \\ 4 & 3 & 3 \\ 8 & 7 & 9}$ found above to solve $\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}$ for $\vect{b} = (4, 10, 24)\T$ and for $\vect{b} = (1, 1, 1)\T$.

**Solution.** For $\vect{b} = (4, 10, 24)\T$, forward substitution with $\M{L}$ gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
y_1 &= 4 \\
y_2 &= 10 - 2(4) = 2 \\
y_3 &= 24 - 4(4) - 3(2) = 2,
\end{aligned}
$$
and back substitution with $\M{U}$ gives $2x_3 = 2$, so $x_3 = 1$; then $x_2 + x_3 = 2$, so $x_2 = 1$; then $2x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 4$, so $x_1 = 1$. So $\vect{x} = (1, 1, 1)\T$.

For $\vect{b} = (1, 1, 1)\T$, the factors are reused, and there is no elimination to repeat. Forward substitution gives $y_1 = 1$, $y_2 = 1 - 2 = -1$ and $y_3 = 1 - 4 - 3(-1) = 0$. Back substitution gives $x_3 = 0$, $x_2 = -1$ and $2x_1 - 1 = 1$, so $x_1 = 1$: $\vect{x} = (1, -1, 0)\T$. Check: $\M{A}(1, -1, 0)\T = (2 - 1, 4 - 3, 8 - 7)\T = (1, 1, 1)\T$. ✓
:::

### Why factorise? Many right-hand sides

Factorising $\M{A}$ costs about $\tfrac{2}{3}n^3$ arithmetic operations, the same as elimination. But the two triangular solves cost only about $n^2$ each. So once $\M{A}$ is factorised, solving for a new right-hand side is cheap. For $n = 1000$, factorising takes about 700 million operations, and each solve afterwards only about 2 million: over 300 times less.

This matters because many problems need the same matrix with many right-hand sides:

- a structure analysed under many different loads, where the matrix describes the structure and each $\vect{b}$ is one set of loads;
- a simulation that moves forward in time, solving a system with the same matrix at every time step;
- computing $\M{A}^{-1}\M{B}$ for a matrix $\M{B}$, one column at a time.

It is also the right way to think about inverses. Instead of computing $\M{A}^{-1}$ and multiplying, factorise $\M{A}$ once and solve whenever a product $\M{A}^{-1}\vect{b}$ is needed (@sec-inverses).

### Row swaps: $\M{P}\M{A} = \M{L}\M{U}$

If elimination meets a zero pivot, it must swap rows, and then $\M{A}$ itself has no $\M{L}\M{U}$ factorisation. The fix is to do all the swaps first, in effect. A **permutation matrix** $\M{P}$ is the identity matrix with its rows in a different order, and $\M{P}\M{A}$ is $\M{A}$ with its rows reordered in the same way. For example, swapping rows 1 and 2 of a $3 \times 3$ matrix is
$$
\M{P} = \mat{0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1}.
$$
Every invertible matrix has a factorisation
$$
\M{P}\M{A} = \M{L}\M{U}.
$$
When a swap happens during elimination, the multipliers already stored in $\M{L}$ for the two rows swap with them, so that each multiplier stays with its row. The app shows this in **Needs a swap**.

Software always swaps rows, even when no pivot is zero: at each step it brings up the row with the **largest** entry in the pivot column. This is called **partial pivoting**, and it keeps rounding errors under control (@sec-pivoting). So the factors that software returns are usually not the ones you find by hand, but they are equally valid. To solve $\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}$, apply the same reordering to $\vect{b}$: solve $\M{L}\vect{y} = \M{P}\vect{b}$, then $\M{U}\vect{x} = \vect{y}$.

::: {#ex-lu-decomposition-2 .callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
### Example 2: a factorisation with a row swap

Find $\M{P}$, $\M{L}$ and $\M{U}$ with $\M{P}\M{A} = \M{L}\M{U}$ for $\M{A} = \mat{0 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 5}$, and use them to find $\det\M{A}$.

**Solution.** The first pivot is 0, so swap rows 1 and 2. Then eliminate: $R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - 2R_1$ (multiplier 2) and, in column 2, $R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - R_2$ (multiplier 1). Row 2 already has a 0 in column 1, so its multiplier is 0.
$$
\mat{0 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 5}
\xrightarrow{R_1 \,\leftrightarrow\, R_2}
\mat{1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 5}
\xrightarrow{R_3 \,\leftarrow\, R_3 - 2R_1}
\mat{1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 3}
\xrightarrow{R_3 \,\leftarrow\, R_3 - R_2}
\mat{1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2}.
$$
So
$$
\M{P} = \mat{0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1},
$$
$$
\M{L} = \mat{1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 1},
$$
$$
\M{U} = \mat{1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2}.
$$
Check row 3 of $\M{L}\M{U}$: $2(1, 1, 1) + 1(0, 2, 1) + 1(0, 0, 2) = (2, 4, 5)$, which is row 3 of $\M{P}\M{A}$. ✓ There was one swap, so
$$
\det\M{A} = -(1 \times 2 \times 2) = -4.
$$
:::

### Determinants for free

Since $\det\M{L} = 1$ (it is triangular with 1s on the diagonal) and $\det\M{U}$ is the product of its diagonal entries (@sec-determinants),
$$
\det\M{A} = \pm\, u_{11}u_{22}\cdots u_{nn},
$$
with a minus sign if an odd number of row swaps were made. This is how software computes determinants.

## In code

SciPy, the scientific companion to NumPy, has the factorisation in `scipy.linalg`. Watch out for one difference of convention: SciPy's `lu` returns $\M{P}$, $\M{L}$, $\M{U}$ with $\M{A} = \M{P}\M{L}\M{U}$, so its $\M{P}$ is the transpose of the $\M{P}$ in $\M{P}\M{A} = \M{L}\M{U}$. MATLAB's `lu` follows the convention of this chapter.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np
import scipy.linalg as sl

A = np.array([[2, 1, 1], [4, 3, 3], [8, 7, 9]])
P, L, U = sl.lu(A)                 # A = P @ L @ U
print(P)
print(np.round(L, 4))
print(np.round(U, 4))
print(np.allclose(P @ L @ U, A))
```

Partial pivoting chose 8, the largest entry in column 1, as the first pivot, so these factors differ from the ones found by hand. For solving, use `lu_factor` once and `lu_solve` for each right-hand side:

```{python}
factors = sl.lu_factor(A)          # the expensive step, done once
for b in ([4, 10, 24], [1, 1, 1]):
    print(np.round(sl.lu_solve(factors, b), 10) + 0)
```

The saving is real. Here 100 right-hand sides are solved for a $1000 \times 1000$ matrix, first by solving from scratch each time, then by factorising once:

```{python}
import time
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
n, k = 1000, 100
M = rng.standard_normal((n, n))
B = rng.standard_normal((n, k))

t0 = time.perf_counter()
for j in range(k):
    np.linalg.solve(M, B[:, j])
t1 = time.perf_counter()
f = sl.lu_factor(M)
for j in range(k):
    sl.lu_solve(f, B[:, j])
t2 = time.perf_counter()
print(f"solve each time: {t1 - t0:.2f} s,  factorise once: {t2 - t1:.2f} s")
```

## MATLAB

```matlab
A = [2 1 1; 4 3 3; 8 7 9];
[L, U, P] = lu(A)            % P*A = L*U

b = [4; 10; 24];
y = L \ (P*b);               % forward substitution
x = U \ y                    % back substitution
```

```{.text .code-output}
L =

    1.0000         0         0
    0.2500    1.0000         0
    0.5000    0.6667    1.0000

U =

    8.0000    7.0000    9.0000
         0   -0.7500   -1.2500
         0         0   -0.6667

P =

     0     0     1
     1     0     0
     0     1     0

x =

     1
     1
     1
```

Partial pivoting chose 8, the largest entry in column 1, as the first pivot, so these factors differ from the ones found by hand. MATLAB's backslash notices that `L` and `U` are triangular, and uses forward and back substitution automatically.

For many right-hand sides, either keep `L`, `U` and `P` and reuse them as above, or use `decomposition`, which stores the factors and reuses them each time you use backslash:

```matlab
dA = decomposition(A, 'lu');
x1 = dA \ [4; 10; 24]
x2 = dA \ [1; 1; 1]
```
:::

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Eliminating a $3 \times 3$ matrix used the multipliers $m_{21} = 3$, $m_{31} = -1$ and $m_{32} = 2$, with no swaps. What is $\M{L}$?

$\M{L} = \mat{1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & 1}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Why is forward substitution with $\M{L}$ so quick?

$\M{L}$ is lower triangular, so its first equation has one unknown, its second has two, and so on. Each unknown is found directly from the ones before it, with no elimination: about $n^2$ operations in all.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Does $\mat{0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0}$ have an LU decomposition?

Not without a row swap: its first pivot is 0. With $\M{P} = \mat{0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0}$, $\M{P}\M{A} = \M{I} = \M{I}\M{I}$, so $\M{L} = \M{U} = \M{I}$.
:::

## Key ideas

- Gaussian elimination factorises $\M{A} = \M{L}\M{U}$: $\M{U}$ is the echelon form, and $\M{L}$ is lower triangular, holding the multipliers.
- To solve $\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}$, solve $\M{L}\vect{y} = \vect{b}$ by forward substitution and then $\M{U}\vect{x} = \vect{y}$ by back substitution.
- Factorising costs about $\tfrac{2}{3}n^3$ operations, but each new right-hand side then costs only about $2n^2$, so factorise once and reuse the factors.
- Software swaps rows as it goes, and computes $\M{P}\M{A} = \M{L}\M{U}$, where $\M{P}$ records the swaps.
- The determinant comes for free: the product of the pivots, with a sign for the swaps.

## In practice

- **Structural engineering**: a finite element model of a building or bridge leads to one large matrix, fixed by the structure, and one right-hand side for each combination of loads (wind, snow, traffic, people). The matrix is factorised once and every load case is solved from the factors.
- **Circuit simulation and other time-stepping methods**: programs that simulate how a circuit or a heat flow changes over time often solve a system with the same matrix at every time step. They factorise it once at the start.
- **Behind the scenes**: `np.linalg.solve`, MATLAB's backslash and `det` all compute an LU factorisation with partial pivoting, using the LAPACK library.

## Going further

- Software stores $\M{L}$ and $\M{U}$ together in one array, overwriting $\M{A}$: the 1s on the diagonal of $\M{L}$ need no storage. This is what `scipy.linalg.lu_factor` returns.
- There are other ways to arrange the same computation. The **Doolittle** method computes $\M{L}$ and $\M{U}$ directly, entry by entry, from $\M{A} = \M{L}\M{U}$; the **Crout** method puts the 1s on the diagonal of $\M{U}$ instead.
- For a symmetric matrix with positive pivots (a **positive definite** matrix), elimination can be arranged so that $\M{U} = \M{L}\T$, giving the **Cholesky factorisation** $\M{A} = \M{L}\M{L}\T$ with half the work and half the storage (@sec-symmetric-matrices).
- For large sparse matrices, those that are mostly zeros, the factors can fill in with many new non-zeros. Reordering the rows and columns cleverly keeps them sparse (@sec-cost-sparse). Why row swaps are needed for accuracy, not just for zero pivots: @sec-pivoting.
- Proof that elimination without swaps gives $\M{A} = \M{L}\M{U}$, and that the factors are unique: @sec-proofs-lu-decomposition.
